description: We are Life Line, a team of students passionate about space, technology, science, and innovation. We’re building health-monitoring software to help astronauts track and understand their health during space missions. We’re looking for motivated teammates with skills in programming, AI/ML, UI/UX, data analysis, research, biology, medicine, or engineering. If you’re creative, collaborative, and excited about space, join us!
summary:
AstroBone is a web-based simulator that predicts bone mineral density (BMD) loss in astronauts during long-duration space missions. In microgravity, the reduced mechanical loading on the skeleton increases bone breakdown, which leads to progressive bone loss. This is a serious concern for missions to the Moon and Mars, where medical equipment and immediate support are limited.
The simulator takes the astronaut’s starting BMD, mission duration, and mission type, together with a selectable resistance exercise plan using the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED). It then models five parts of the bone-remodelling process: bone-forming cells, bone-breaking cells, their precursor cells, new bone material, and mineralized bone. Two simpler models are included for comparison, and a sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions affect the results most.
AstroBone helps astronauts and mission planners compare exercise strategies and understand why bone loss occurs. It runs in a browser without installation or a continuous internet connection. It provides estimates, not medical diagnoses.
details:
AstroBone is a website that contains a simulator that helps to predict bone mineral density (BMD) loss in astronauts during long-duration space missions. In gravity, the mechanical loading on the skeleton is significantly reduced, which increases bone resorption and can actually lead to bone loss over time. The simulator is intended to help astronauts and mission planners help estimate and understand this process.

The simulator has four main stages:

  1. The actual astronaut information: The user enters the astronaut’s initial BMD, his age, his mission duration, and his mission type. Age is currently stored as background information only and is not used in the calculations.
  2. Mission Conditions: The simulator accounts for the level of mechanical loading, which is connected with the selected environment. Users can help choose between an orbital space station mission, a Moon environment, and a Mars round trip.
  3. Exercise and Countermeasures: Users can help adjust the intensity and duration of resistance exercise performed with the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED). The anti-resorptive effect can also be used to see how reducing bone breakdown affects the predicted results.
  4. Mathematical Predictions: Three mathematical models are used to predict changes in BMD. The primary model describes five parts of the bone-remodelling process: osteoblasts, osteoclasts, their precursor cells, newly formed bone matrix, and mineralized bone. Two simpler models are included for comparison.

After a simulation is completed, the user can view graphs of predicted BMD, compare to different exercise plans, examine the response of bone cells over time, and can help analyze how different scientific assumptions affect the results.

Benefits and Intended Impact of this app for health monitoring.

  • Early Awareness: Helps astronauts understand the possible amount of bone loss before and during a mission.
  • Predictive Monitoring: Estimates how BMD can actually change over periods of days and months.
  • Personalized Simulations: Allows the starting BMD, mission conditions, and exercise plans to be adjusted.
  • Improved Decision-Making: Helps mission planners compare exercise strategies using the same model.
  • Understanding Bone Loss: Shows how bone-forming and bone-breaking cells respond to different levels of microgravity.
  • Scientific Transparency: Displays the models, assumptions, and limitations behind each prediction.
  • Accessibility: Runs in a web browser without installation or an account, and the simulation can run on the device without an actual continuous internet connection.

The main goal of AstroBone is to help support the understanding and planning of astronaut bone health, particularly during long-duration missions where access to medical equipment and immediate support is limited, overtime we will add other simulations to support the health of other parts of the body, but we have decided to choose bones first as it’s one of the most affected when your at space.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Used to build the structure, appearance, and layout of the website, and to develop the numerical model simulation, calculations, and interactive features.
  • Chart.js: Used to create interactive graphs and display simulation results.
  • RK45 Numerical Solver: is used to calculate how the five bone-remodelling variables change over time.
  • Bisection Method: Used to find the lowest exercise intensity that keeps bone loss within a selected limit.
  • Node.js: Used to helped to make automated tests and use the numerical engine.

The original prototype used Python with NumPy and SciPy for numerical calculations. The current version runs entirely in a web browser.

Creativity of the Project

AstroBone combines biology, mathematics, and software in a single website. Rather than only reporting how much bone density an astronaut may lose, this simulator also explains why the loss happens by showing how bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells interact under reduced loading.

The application can be used in different space missions, and exercise plans can be compared within the same simulation. Users can help modify parameter values, test alternative assumptions, and actually help observe how these changes affect the final predictions. A sensitivity analysis is included to identify which assumptions have the greatest influence on the results, which makes the simulator more transparent and allows users to examine its predictions critically.

Factors to be considered

My team considered some of the following scientific factors during the development of our project:

  • How reduced gravity affects the amount of stress placed on bones and causes bone loss.
  • How osteoblasts and osteoclasts work together to build and break down bone tissue.
  • How exercise and physical activity can help prevent bone loss.
  • How the length of a space mission and different gravity levels affect bone health.
  • Using NASA research and scientific studies to support the findings.
  • Making sure the mathematical models are accurate and that the calculations are based on realistic assumptions.
  • The lack of medical equipment, such as bone density scanners, during long space missions.
  • Creating a browser-based application that can still work with limited or no internet access.

Limitations

AstroBone provides mathematical estimates and not actual medical measurements or diagnoses from doctors. Some model values rely on assumptions because published data were not available. Further testing and validation using real astronaut data would be required before the simulator could be used for medical decision-making.
